score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/central trust-ledger framing, 5 stays promise-first and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: Strong local audit evidence and boundary separation make this a good fit for peer-local assessment, but the design still speaks in claim-card/conformance terms more than Promise-Theory-native promises.
strengths: Direct support for peer-local observations via local promise-accounting records.
Clear separation between live, audit, storage, and device planes.
Exact immutable audit anchors improve later human and LLM auditability.
Good failure posture for ambiguous non-idempotent effects through break-witnesses.
weaknesses: Promise vocabulary is weaker than the underlying PT behavior.
The artifact set is slightly heavier than the scenario needs for simple local pull/keep/advertise decisions.
Shared app identity and authoritative-boundary fields may invite over-global interpretation.
risks: Claim-card framing may drift toward normative conformance bundles instead of small explicit promises.
Authoritative-boundary identity language could be read as stronger or more centralized than local trust warrants.
Local append-only audit records can grow into ledger-heavy wrappers if not kept minimal.
open_questions: Can the scoped claim card be rewritten as explicit first-person agent promises rather than a conformance-style artifact?
For peer-local pull/keep/advertise decisions, which claim-card fields are actually necessary beyond local observations and cited audit anchors?
When no frozen pCID exists, does draft-path plus revision-hash introduce too much authority framing for a supposedly local-trust design?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.

autonomous_agents.note: Peers publish their own scoped artifacts and keep local append-only records; break-witness handling preserves autonomous refusal under uncertainty.

scoped_intent.note: Scope by plane is strong, but the core artifact is a claim card rather than explicit promise-first declarations of intent.

no_promises_for_others.note: Mostly respected, but shared app-family and claim-card framing can blur who is actually promising what unless each embodiment states its own first-person intent.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: The design explicitly distinguishes hash/address, request receipt, retention, and physical-effect completion, avoiding guaranteed-outcome language.

local_trust_assessment.note: Strong fit here: Alice can rely on local observations, audit anchors, and promise-accounting records without any token-transfer requirement.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: The design separates possession, retrieval, retention, and authorization; using or requesting data is not treated as an obligation on others.

violations: Uses claim/conformance-style vocabulary instead of consistently first-person promise wording.
Multi-embodiment/shared-family framing risks reading as umbrella claims unless each agent publishes its own scoped promise.
